ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached figure shows a 3×3 grid. The number 1 has been filled in the upper-left square, that is, r1c1=1; the number 2 has been filled in the very middle square, that is, r2c2=2. The gray squares are located in the middle and bottom of the right column, that is, r2c3 and r3c3. Reasoning: Each row and each column must contain exactly 1, 2, 3. Look at r1c2: it is in row 1, and row 1 already has 1, so r1c2 can only be 2 or 3; it is also in column 2, and column 2 already has the 2 in the center square, so r1c2 can only be 1 or 3. Under the common restriction of the two, r1c2=3. Thus row 1 already has r1c1=1 and r1c2=3, so r1c3=2. method.method_draft: Describe the image as a 3x3 grid with 1 in the top-left cell, 2 in the center cell, and the grey cells in the middle-right and bottom-right positions. Let the cell positions be r(row)c(column). From the text, each row and column must contain 1, 2, 3 exactly once. Since r1c2 is in row 1, where 1 is already used, it can only be 2 or 3. Since r1c2 is also in column 2, where 2 is already used at the center, it can only be 1 or 3. Therefore r1c2 = 3. Then row 1 must have r1c3 = 2. Column 3 must contain 1, 2, 3, whose sum is 6. Since the top cell of column 3 is 2, the two grey cells in that column sum to 6 - 2 = 4.
